title: Scale out: identical stateless servers behind one address
caption: Clients only know the load balancer. Servers can be added, removed or fail without clients noticing.

steps.text: DNS now points at the load balancer. The app servers sit on private addresses that clients never see.
The LB spreads requests across the pool. Three servers give roughly three times the capacity, and you add a fourth when load grows.
Servers keep no session state of their own. Sessions and data live in shared stores, so any server can answer any request.
App 2 fails its health checks: the LB stops sending it traffic, and App 1 and App 3 absorb the load.

scenarios.name: A server dies
scenarios.summary: Health checks eject the dead server within seconds; the rest of the pool absorbs its share, so you need headroom (N+1).

steps.text: Traffic is spread evenly: each of the three servers takes about a third.
App 2 crashes. Requests already in flight on it fail or time out.
After three missed health checks (~15 s) the LB ejects App 2 and stops routing to it.
App 1 and App 3 now take half each: 50% more load per server. Size the pool so N-1 servers can carry peak.

scenarios.name: Sticky sessions
scenarios.summary: Pinning a user to one server breaks even spreading: one hot user or a server restart hurts. Keep session state in a shared store instead.

steps.text: The LB sets a cookie so each user always lands on the same server (its in-memory session lives there).
One hot user (a bot, a big tenant) sends 10× normal traffic. All of it hits App 1, while App 2 and App 3 sit idle.
App 1 is redeployed: every session pinned to it is gone, and those users are logged out.
Fix: move sessions to a shared store and drop stickiness, so any server can serve any request again.

scenarios.name: Alternative: DNS round robin
scenarios.summary: No load balancer: DNS hands out all server IPs. Free and simple, but a dead server keeps getting traffic until clients' DNS caches expire.

steps.text: DNS returns all three IPs in rotating order; each client picks the first.
Clients connect straight to the servers: load spreads roughly evenly, with no extra hop or box.
App 3 dies. DNS has no health checks, and resolvers cache the answer for the TTL: some users keep hitting a dead IP.
Good enough for internal tools or as the first split across LB nodes; not as the only failover for a product.

scenarios.name: Risk: LB is a SPOF
scenarios.summary: One load balancer just moves the single point of failure. Run an active/passive pair sharing a floating IP (VRRP) so a standby takes over.

steps.text: All traffic goes to one virtual IP, owned by the active LB.
The passive LB watches the active one through a heartbeat every second.
The active LB dies. Without a standby, every user is down, however many app servers are healthy.
Heartbeats stop; within ~3 s the passive LB claims the VIP and traffic flows again. Clients keep the same address.
